title: Frankfort: Frank's Ford becomes the capital
summary: Frankfort began as a buffalo-trail ford named for Stephen Frank, killed there in 1780, and in 1792 it was chosen as Kentucky's capital.
bodyMarkdown:
Before Frankfort was a town, the site was a ford across the Kentucky River on one of the great buffalo trails. English explorers were in the [Frankfort](https://grokipedia.com/page/Frankfort,_Kentucky) area by the early 1750s. The crossing later gave the capital its name.

## Frank's Ford

The account most often repeated says the name came from a fight in 1780. A group of settlers from [Bryan's Station](/stories/bryan-station-siege-august-1782/) was on its way to make salt at [Mann's Lick](/stories/manns-lick-louisvilles-salt-town/) when Native warriors attacked them at the river. Pioneer Stephen Frank was killed, and settlers called the crossing "Frank's Ford." The name was later shortened to Frankfort.

The [City of Frankfort's history](https://www.frankfort.ky.gov/323/City-History) and the [Grokipedia article on Frankfort](https://grokipedia.com/page/Frankfort,_Kentucky) both tell it that way.

A marker at River View Park words the same tradition differently. It says the name commemorates Stephen Frank, killed in a skirmish between hunters and Native warriors, and that his campsite was known locally as Frank's Ford.

Another tradition links the name to [Frankfurt am Main](https://grokipedia.com/page/Frankfurt). A 2025 essay on the name quotes a Kentucky Historical Society marker that records both ideas and treats Frank's Ford as what many people believe, not as a settled fact. The [Northern Kentucky Tribune essay](https://nkytribune.com/2025/04/our-rich-history-frankfort-kentucky-a-german-place-name/) says the Kentucky Encyclopedia tells the Frank's Ford story, and it argues that the story is legend and that the German name is the more plausible one.

The city's own history still repeats Frank's Ford. The name is traditional, and the sources do not agree on which tradition to trust.

## Wilkinson's town

In 1786 James Wilkinson bought land on the north side of the river, the ground that became downtown Frankfort. That year the Virginia legislature set aside 100 acres as the town of Frankfort. The city's history says those acres were his. He promoted the town as a future capital.

He believed farm produce could go down the Kentucky River to the Ohio and the Mississippi and on to New Orleans.

Daniel Gano and Daniel Weisiger helped lay the settlement out. An [ExploreKYHistory essay on Daniel Weisiger](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/610) says that in the late 1780s he helped Wilkinson lay out and name the streets. A [Northern Kentucky Tribune essay](https://nkytribune.com/2025/04/our-rich-history-frankfort-kentucky-a-german-place-name/), citing the 1874 History of Kentucky, says Gano, a Revolutionary captain who came out with Wilkinson, and Weisiger laid the town out in 1787. Attacks slowed the first years, and growth in the late 1780s was slow.

Weisiger became Frankfort's first postmaster. The ExploreKYHistory essay dates that service from October 1, 1794, to July 1, 1795. By the fall of 1794 the town had a United States post office.

In 1792 Wilkinson sold his Frankfort land. The buyer carried the town's offer to the commissioners.

## Choosing a capital

Kentucky became the 15th state on June 1, 1792. The first constitution had been adopted at [Danville](/stories/danville-and-constitution-square/) on April 19. It did not name a capital. Article X told the House of Representatives, at its 1792 session, to choose 21 people by ballot.

The members present from Mercer County and Fayette County would then take turns striking one name, until five were left. Any three of those five, agreeing, could fix the seat of government, take grants of land, make terms with the owners, and lay off a town. They were to swear that they would do it in the way most beneficial to the state at large.

The seat they fixed would stand unless two-thirds of both houses later moved it. The text is in the [Secretary of State's copy of the 1792 constitution](https://web.sos.ky.gov/ofx/timeline?id=1).

The General Assembly met at [Lexington](/stories/lexington-named/) on June 4, 1792. That was the day Isaac Shelby reached town to be inaugurated as the first governor.

The 1874 history is Richard H. Collins's enlargement of his father Lewis Collins's 1847 Historical Sketches. The title page of [volume 1](https://archive.org/details/collinshistoricav01coll) says the son revised his father's book and brought it down to 1874.

Richard H. Collins dates the choice of the five commissioners to June 18. The [Kentucky Historical Society marker](https://history.ky.gov/markers/frankfort-chosen-as-capital) dates their appointment to June 20. The names agree. John Allen and John Edwards were both of Bourbon County. Henry Lee was of Mason County.

Thomas Kennedy was of Madison County. Robert Todd was of Fayette County. An 1881 history of Franklin County names the same five.

Through the summer and fall they visited the places that had made offers. Collins and that 1881 history name the same list: Legerwood's Bend in Mercer County, Delany's Ferry and Petersburg in Woodford County, Louisville, Lexington, Frankfort, and [Leestown](/stories/leestown/), a mile downriver.

The marker adds that each hopeful town offered a list of contributions, which was the custom, and that the commissioners looked the sites over before they voted. A marker at River View Park says the four sites given the most serious consideration were Petersburg, Leestown, Lexington, and Frankfort. The Grokipedia article on Frankfort names Lexington and Washington among the places considered, and it does not give the longer list.

Washington is not on the marker or in Collins. Boonesborough, and Danville, where the statehood conventions had met, are not on those lists of bidders.

What the other towns offered, item by item, is not in these accounts. Frankfort's offer is. The marker says the town won by perseverance and, according to early histories, by the offer made through Andrew Holmes, who had bought the tract from James Wilkinson that year: his log house as a capitol for seven years, town lots, £50 worth of locks and hinges, 10 boxes of glass, 1,500 pounds of nails, and $3,000 in gold.

Collins itemizes a longer proposition. Holmes would convey, for seven years, the house and tenement lately occupied by James Wilkinson. He would convey the lots marked as public ground, numbers 58, 59, 68, 74, 75, 79, 83, and 84.

He offered a choice of 30 unsold lots, or half of the 74 still unsold, and, if more ground was needed, half of 50 further acres laid into half-acre lots. He offered the warehouse rents for seven years. He offered 10 boxes of 10-by-12 window glass, 1,500 pounds of nails, £50 worth of locks and hinges, and stone and scantling delivered on the public ground.

In place of that stone and scantling the same account offers stone for 1,590 perches of wall, the use of his sawmill, a carriage, a wagon, and two horses until enough scantling was sawed, and timber from his tract.

The River View Park marker compresses the same gift. It says Frankfort, then a town of about 200 people, offered ten boxes of glass, 1,500 pounds of nails, the use of a sawmill, two horses and a cart, a donation of land, and 166 2/3 dollars' worth of locks and hinges, stone, and lumber, and that this made Frankfort the highest bidder. That dollar figure is the other marker's £50.

Separate from the deed, Collins records a bond dated August 9, 1792, signed by eight Frankfort residents, to pay the commissioners $3,000 in gold or silver. The 1881 county history sums the gift up as $3,000 in gold, the ground, the first state house, and town lots.

The house is not described the same way twice. The capital marker and the Grokipedia article on Frankfort call it a log house. Collins calls it the house Wilkinson had lately occupied, and does not say it was log. The 1881 history calls it a large two-story frame in the western end of north Frankfort, in the bend of the river, and says it stood until 1870.

On December 5, 1792, meeting in Lexington, the commissioners resolved that Frankfort was the most proper place for the seat of government. Collins says John Edwards was absent, that two of the board, Robert Todd among them, favored Lexington, and that two favored Frankfort. Any three had to agree. Collins says Todd lived in Lexington and owned a great deal of land nearby, changed his vote so that no one could say his interest had decided it, and that the change gave Frankfort the three votes it needed.

The marker does not tell that story. It says that, by a majority, the commissioners recommended Frankfort to the legislature in Lexington that day. The 1881 history records the December 5 decision and does not mention a switched vote. The story of the changed vote rests on Collins.

The legislature approved the report on December 8. On December 22 it adjourned to hold its next sessions in the house of Andrew Holmes at Frankfort. The 1881 history says the next legislature opened there in November 1793. [ExploreKYHistory](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/505) says lawmakers met in Holmes's house, the one that had been Wilkinson's, until the first capitol was finished in 1794.

The [state capitol history](https://historicproperties.ky.gov/hp/ncs/Pages/ch.aspx) dates that first building to 1793–1794, a rough stone house of three stories on the public square. The River View marker dates a first permanent statehouse to 1796. The year the first capitol opened is not the same in every account.

## Why Frankfort

The reasons given for the choice are not one sentence.

The constitution told the commissioners to pick the place most beneficial to the state, and to take the help landowners would give. ExploreKYHistory says they were charged to find the most suitable ground and the most assistance toward a capitol, and that Holmes's pledge of land, money, and materials ran far ahead of the other bids. The Kentucky Historical Society marker says Frankfort won by perseverance and by that offer, "according to early histories."

Collins says the proposition that induced the location was Holmes's conveyance plus the $3,000 bond. The River View marker calls Frankfort the highest bidder.

The state capitol history gives a different kind of reason. It calls Frankfort centrally placed in the Bluegrass, on the S-curve of the Kentucky River, and it says the state, in return for the land, contracted to fix the seat there unless two-thirds of the legislature moved it. The Grokipedia article on Frankfort gives the navigable river, and the trade it promised, as a reason beside Holmes's house.

That river argument is also the one Wilkinson had been making since he laid the town out. Later writers state it. It is not a line in the resolution Collins quotes, which says only that Frankfort was the most proper place.

A [modern summary of Kentucky](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/geography-and-cartography/kentucky) says the choice was a compromise, because Louisville and Lexington both wanted the honor and Frankfort sits between them. That is not how Collins tells the 1792 vote. Louisville was one bidder among several. The split he describes was between Lexington and Frankfort, broken when Robert Todd left the Lexington side.

Calling the capital a compromise between Lexington and Louisville is a later shorthand, not the ballot the early histories describe.

## Kept, and challenged

The choice did not end the argument. When the capitol burned in 1813, Collins dates the fire to November 25 and says friends of Frankfort subscribed $20,000 toward a new building. ExploreKYHistory says the legislature considered leaving and that the gifts kept the seat in Frankfort. A second capitol, finished in 1816, burned in 1824.

On January 12, 1827, the General Assembly voted to build again. A [Legislative Research Commission note](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/LegislativeMoments/moments04RS/12_web_leg_history.html) says the act put up $20,000 in money and supplies, and that the men in charge chose the Greek Revival plan of Gideon Shryock. The [National Register nomination](https://npgallery.nps.gov/GetAsset/5c315ff3-af39-4973-bd66-5fb88f28fe5a) says he was 25 when he entered that design. The [Old State Capitol](https://grokipedia.com/page/old_state_capitol_kentucky) housed the General Assembly from 1830.

The same legislative note says lawmakers first met there in December 1829, while it was still unfinished, and that it served until the new capitol was dedicated in 1910. The [marker on the Old State House](https://history.ky.gov/markers/old-state-house) says the building served until the new capitol of 1909. It has been the home of the Kentucky Historical Society since 1920.

A [National Park Service guide to capitol landmarks](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalhistoriclandmarks/upload/Capitols_NHLs_Resource_Guide_Final.pdf) lists the Old State House as a National Historic Landmark designated in 1971.

Lexington and Louisville were not finished with the question. The state capitol history says the two cities kept contending for the capital after the Civil War, and that the constitution of 1891 settled it. [Section 255](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/Law/Constitution/Constitution/ViewConstitution?rsn=292) says the seat shall continue in Frankfort unless two-thirds of each house of the first General Assembly after that constitution voted to remove it. It was not removed.

## A house in the new capital

In 1796 John Brown, one of Kentucky's first United States senators, built [Liberty Hall](/stories/liberty-hall-john-browns-frankfort-house/) in Frankfort. Frankfort is still the capital. In the 2020 census it had 28,602 people.
